readingGuide.purpose: Registry description: declared intent, not proof of vendor behavior. Consult the evidence dossier for supported consumer claims and limits.
readingGuide.features: Registry guidance tags for search and grouping. Tags are not applicability predicates; an empty list means no tags were supplied.
readingGuide.applicability: Current metadata page-type gate. Unrestricted does not mean unconditional: evidence requirements and audit body guards still apply. Article is distinct from unknown/general; legacy content input normalizes to unknown in runScan.
readingGuide.scoring: Weight is intrinsic evidence mass, not guaranteed score impact. na and informative results do not score. Detected-only typed matches remain informative. In mixed scans, declared matches provide the primary result and detected matches remain in advisoryResults; only the primary result can contribute weight. Experimental audits need opt-in.
readingGuide.requires: Current scan-evidence requirements from registry metadata. Artifact presence and feature guards belong in the audit or gatherer, not in this list.
readingGuide.references: Paths are relative to the repository root. source is the audit implementation; test is its adjacent test file, not a coverage claim. dossier governs the evidence grade and consumer claims.
readingGuide.maintenance: Generated by pnpm build:audit-map; verify with pnpm check:audit-map. Edit source metadata or the dossier, then regenerate. Do not hand-edit generated active records.

audits.title: AI crawler vs conversational agent separation
audits.purpose: Not all AI bots are the same. Training crawlers like GPTBot, CCBot, and Google-Extended scrape your content to build datasets, while conversational and retrieval agents like ChatGPT-User, Claude-User, and OAI-SearchBot fetch pages live to answer real user questions and can send referral traffic back to you. Many sites want to block the former while welcoming the latter — but a single catch-all User-agent: * cannot express that distinction. Granular robots.txt governance names both categories explicitly so each gets the access policy you actually intend.

audits.title: Documented AI bots allowed by robots.txt
audits.purpose: Reports your robots.txt stance on five long-tail AI bot tokens in one place. Only the bots whose operator publishes crawler documentation — YouBot (You.com) and AI2Bot (Allen Institute) — affect the score, because only those directives have a documented reader. Bytespider, cohere-ai and Diffbot are listed for information: blocking them is a legitimate operational choice that costs no AI-answer visibility.

audits.title: AI usage-preference declaration
audits.purpose: Where a site declares how AI systems may use its content. The IETF AIPREF work attaches that preference to a Content-Usage response header or a robots.txt rule, and explicitly leaves the HTML head out of scope; the head-level noai/noimageai convention has real adoption but no AI vendor documents honoring it. This audit reports what a site declares and where, and never treats declaring nothing as a defect.

audits.title: AI crawlers get the same response from the edge that browsers get
audits.purpose: Fetches the homepage, sampled content URLs and /llms.txt once as a browser and once per published AI crawler User-Agent, then classifies every difference: Cloudflare challenge, pay-per-crawl 402, proof-of-work wall, rate limit, opaque 403, or a 200 carrying a fraction of the text. Reports per crawler and per URL, and scores a block only where robots.txt said the crawler was welcome.

audits.title: AI usage signals agree across every channel that carries them
audits.purpose: Normalizes every AI-usage signal the site emits — robots.txt Allow/Disallow for training crawlers, AIPREF Content-Usage, Cloudflare Content-Signal, TDM-Rep in its three transports, and inline RSL permits/prohibits — into one comparable model, and reports where two channels contradict each other for the same category over overlapping paths.

audits.title: AIPREF Content-Usage declarations are valid and can be read
audits.purpose: Parses every `Content-Usage` declaration — in robots.txt at file scope and inside each group, and in the response header — as the RFC 8941 dictionary AIPREF defines, validates its categories and values, and checks that the paths it attaches to are actually crawlable. A preference attached to a disallowed path has no effect: attach-05 gives disallowed paths no usage preferences at all.

audits.title: Amazonbot allowed
audits.purpose: Reads the robots.txt rules that apply to Amazonbot — its own group if it has one, otherwise the catch-all — and reports whether they let it fetch the site root. A named group is not required: under RFC 9309 §2.2.1 an open catch-all grants the same access.

audits.title: ClaudeBot crawl access
audits.purpose: ClaudeBot collects web content that may contribute to Anthropic's model training, and Anthropic states its bots honour robots.txt. This check reads the robots.txt rules that actually apply to ClaudeBot — its own group if it has one, otherwise the catch-all — and reports whether they let it fetch the site root. A named group is not required: under RFC 9309 §2.2.1 an open catch-all grants the same access. The legacy `anthropic-ai` and `Claude-Web` tokens are reported when present but never scored, because Anthropic's current crawler documentation names neither.

audits.title: Applebot-Extended allowed
audits.purpose: Applebot-Extended is a robots.txt usage-control token, not a crawler: no request carries it. This check reads the rules that apply to it — its own group if it has one, otherwise the catch-all — and reports whether they disallow the site root. A named group is not required: under RFC 9309 §2.2.1 an open catch-all grants the same permission.

audits.title: Content served to AI crawlers matches the browser, or is declared
audits.purpose: Fetches sampled content URLs as a browser and as GPTBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot, then measures the difference two ways — main-text length ratio and 5-gram shingle similarity — because a stub and a rewritten page look identical on length alone. Where a difference exists, requires Google's restricted-content markup and checks that the declared cssSelector resolves against the served DOM.

audits.title: Bravebot allowed
audits.purpose: Reads the robots.txt rules that apply to Bravebot — its own group if it has one, otherwise the catch-all — and reports whether they let it fetch the site root. A named group is not required: under RFC 9309 §2.2.1 an open catch-all grants the same access.

audits.title: Canonical URLs point at the right page
audits.purpose: A `<link rel="canonical">` tells crawlers which URL is the authoritative version of a page, and the URL they pick is the one eligible to be shown — and cited — in AI answers. The value matters more than the presence: pages that all canonicalize onto the homepage remove themselves from the index.

audits.title: CCBot allowed
audits.purpose: Reads the robots.txt rules that apply to CCBot — its own group if it has one, otherwise the catch-all — and reports whether they let it fetch the site root. A named group is not required: under RFC 9309 §2.2.1 an open catch-all grants the same access.

audits.purpose: Reads the robots.txt rules that apply to ChatGPT-User — its own group if it has one, otherwise the catch-all — and reports whether they let it fetch the site root. A named group is not required: under RFC 9309 §2.2.1 an open catch-all grants the same access.

audits.title: Claude-SearchBot allowed
audits.purpose: Reads the robots.txt rules that apply to Claude-SearchBot — its own group if it has one, otherwise the catch-all — and reports whether they let it fetch the site root. A named group is not required: under RFC 9309 §2.2.1 an open catch-all grants the same access.
